newsitem.title: GERMANY: Poland wants to be in future talks on NATO-report.
newsitem.headline: Poland wants to be in future talks on NATO-report.

text.p: Poland's President Aleksander Kwasniewski was quoted on Thursday as demanding that NATO consults Poland on any future agreements with Russia over stationing military infrastructure on its territory.
"We expect to take part in the next NATO talks," Kwasniewski said in an interview with Germany's Der Spiegel news weekly, released ahead of publication on Saturday.

Kwasniewski said it was unclear what had been decided by Presidents Boris Yeltsin and Bill Clinton at their summit in Helsinki last week with regard to NATO infrastructure on the soil of Russia's former allies.
Yeltsin and Clinton vowed to press ahead with a NATO-Russia charter to set out a new relationship between Russia and the pact.

NATO pledged not to move nuclear weapons onto the territory of new members and not to threaten Russian security with military movements to the East. Kwasniewski said he wanted to know what these agreements actually meant for Poland.

Kwasniewski said he had discussed the issue of deployment of weapons and troops to potential new members with NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, who is due to travel to Moscow next month for talks on the subject.
"He (Solana) did not have any exact ideas about what should happen to military infrastructure. We expect that NATO will consult Poland on all these questions," he said.
Poland has been anxious that NATO should not agree on a watered-down NATO membership for new entrants to meet Russian objections that the pact's enlargement threatens its security.
Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are leading candidates to be invited to begin membership negotiations at the NATO summit in Madrid in July.
Kwasniewski said he thought a solution could be found to the question of the massive military arsenal stationed in Russia's western enclave of Kaliningrad, bordering Poland.
He said if Poland was to stay a zone without nuclear weapons then his country would lay "great weight" on Kaliningrad also staying nuclear-free.
Kwasniewski stressed Poland was very keen to work with Russia, but only as an "equal-ranking partner".
